query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a thin copper (Cu) interlayer between high-entropy alloy (HEA) layers will enable a controlled transition from diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep by modulating interface coherency.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA multilayers with coherent interfaces and no Cu interlayer.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a thin, systematically varied Cu interlayer between HEA layers.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature and stress conditions where both diffusion-controlled (e.g., Nabarro–Herring or Coble creep) and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms can be active.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of interface coherency modulated by the Cu interlayer, which provides an intermediate lattice parameter and diffusivity between the HEA layers.
generation.mechanism: Copper’s relatively high self-diffusivity and its intermediate lattice parameter reduce coherency strains at the HEA interfaces, lowering the barrier for dislocation nucleation. This controlled change in interfacial structure is expected to shift the dominant creep mechanism from atomic (diffusion) mediated processes at thinner or absent interlayers toward dislocation-mediated deformation as the Cu interlayer thickness increases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with an optimally thick Cu interlayer will show a measurable shift in creep behavior, marked by reduced diffusion-mediated creep rates and increased signatures of dislocation activity (e.g., higher dislocation density, characteristic deformation features) compared to HEA multilayers without the Cu layer.
generation.baseline: HEA multilayers without the Cu interlayer, which are predicted to predominantly exhibit diffusion-mediated creep under the test conditions.
generation.boundary: The effect is anticipated over a certain range of Cu interlayer thicknesses. Too thin a Cu layer may not sufficiently modify the interface, while an overly thick layer may disrupt overall structural coherence or introduce other deformation modes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold Cu thickness required for the transition and the quantitative degree of creep mechanism shift are uncertain and likely depends on the specific HEA composition and testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of HEA multilayer samples with various controlled Cu interlayer thicknesses, including a control sample with no Cu. Subject all samples to identical high-temperature creep testing under moderate stress. Use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and in situ mechanical testing to examine the interface coherency and the active creep mechanisms.
measurements: Dislocation density and morphology via electron microscopy
Interface structure and coherency using HRTEM
Activation energy derived from creep testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiment shows no systematic change in creep mechanism—with no observable increase in dislocation-mediated behaviors (such as dislocation density or altered creep rate trends) with increasing Cu interlayer thickness relative to the control sample—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6

frame.system: High‐entropy alloy multilayers designed as advanced coating materials with highly controlled (coherent) interfaces.
frame.goal: To understand and tune the creep behavior by deliberately engineering an interface that mediates the change from diffusion‐mediated (e.g., Nabarro–Herring or Coble creep) to dislocation‐mediated (power‐law) creep mechanisms.
frame.limitation: The role that interfacial coherency plays in controlling which creep mechanism dominates is not clearly established, leaving uncertainty about how to design multilayers that reliably switch between the two regimes.
root_cause_cues: transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms
constraints: the transition layer must be chemically and crystallographically compatible with the HEA multilayers
it must allow for a change in the dominant deformation mechanism (from diffusion-based at lower stresses/higher temperatures to dislocation-based at higher stresses or with thicker layers)
the material should maintain strong, coherent bonding at the interfaces to reflect the design intent of the multilayer
frame.regime: Elevated temperature and stress conditions where both diffusion (atomic rearrangements) and dislocation (line defects) creep can be activated, typically in the microstructurally controlled nanoscale regime.
prior_attempts: Studies on classical multilayer systems (e.g., Cu/Nb nanolaminates) have shown that very thin layers and coherent interfaces can cause a shift in the deformation mode; however, these insights have not been fully translated to HEA multilayers where the complex chemistry may modify diffusion and dislocation characteristics.
frame.understanding: There is a need to elucidate how an interlayer material can act as a transition element. For instance, incorporating a material like copper (Cu) – which in established systems (e.g., Cu/Nb nanolaminates) has been shown to support a switch between diffusion‐mediated and dislocation‐mediated creep due to its relatively high self-diffusivity and propensity for dislocation activity under different regimes – could be a promising approach. Copper’s role would be to offer an intermediate lattice parameter and diffusivity that, when integrated as an interlayer, may effectively modulate interface coherency. This modulation can tune the balance between diffusion and dislocation creep mechanisms, thereby clarifying and controlling the creep response in HEA multilayers.

decision.trend: Recent work on HEAs has focused on tailoring mechanical properties via compositional tuning and advanced processing (e.g., additive manufacturing, high‐pressure treatments) while achieving high strength, ductility, and oxidation resistance. In parallel, classical multilayer studies (like Cu/Nb nanolaminates) have demonstrated that very thin, coherent interlayers can trigger a switch between diffusion‐mediated and dislocation‐mediated creep regimes. However, despite extensive work on HEA synthesis and property enhancement, the deliberate use of a transition layer to control the creep mechanism via interface coherency has not yet been directly pursued in HEA multilayers.
decision.unsolved: The challenge remains to design a transition layer that is both chemically and crystallographically compatible with HEA multilayers and that can effectively mediate a switch from diffusion‐based to dislocation‐based creep under service conditions.
decision.lever: Integrate and systematically vary a thin copper (Cu) interlayer between HEA layers
decision.why: Copper is known from classical Cu/Nb systems to have an intermediate lattice parameter and relatively high self-diffusivity, making it a promising candidate to modulate interface coherency. This lever allows researchers to precisely control the interlayer thickness and spacing to promote the transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms and verify the effect in HEA multilayers.
